sections.heading: ABSTRACT
sections.text:
Mesoporous Cu foams formed by a template assisted electrodeposition process have been
identified as CO2 electrocatalysts that are highly selective towards C2 product formation (C2H4, C2H6) with C2 efficiencies reaching FEC2 = 55%. The partial current of C2 product formation was found to be higher than the one of the (parasitic) hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) at any
potential studied (-0.4 to -1.0 vs RHE). Moreover, formate production could largely be
suppressed at any applied potential down to efficiencies of FEformate ≤ 6%. A key point of the Cu foam catalyst activation is the in operando reduction of a Cu2O phase thereby creating a high abundance of surface sites active for C-C coupling. The cuprous oxide
phase has been formed after the Cu electrodeposition step by exposing the high-surface area
catalyst to air at RT.
The superior selectivity of the Cu foam catalyst studied herein originates from a combination of
two effects, firstly the availability of specific surface sites for C-C coupling (dominant (100)
surface texture) and secondly the temporal trapping of gaseous intermediates (in particular CO
and C2H4) inside the mesoporous catalyst material during the CO2 electrolysis. A systematic CO2 electrolysis study reveals a strong dependence of the C2 efficiencies on the particular surface pore size of the mesoporous Cu catalysts with a maximum in the FEC2 between 50 and 100 µm pore diameter.
KEYWORDS. Carbon dioxide, electroreduction, copper foam catalysts, Faradaic efficiency, pH
change

1. Introduction
The electrochemical reduction of CO2 (in the following referred to as CO2RR) into products of higher value such as high energy density fuels 1 (methanol 2 , ethanol) or other useful feedstock chemicals (ethene 3 , CO/H2 (syngas) 3a, 4 , formic acid 3a, 5 ) has attracted tremendous interest over the last decades in both, fundamental science and the development of chemical process technologies. 6 Such CO2 electroreduction would offer the unique chance to close the anthropogenic CO2 cycle, in particular by using excesses of renewable energies from solar, wind and hydro sources (power to value concept). 7 Efficiencies of CO2 conversion are, however, strongly limited by the high overpotentials needed to activate the CO2 reactant. In particular when using aqueous media, the CO2 conversion is superimposed by the (parasitic) water splitting reaction thus significantly reducing the overall CO2 conversion efficiency. 3a Catalysts are required not only to reduce such overpotentials but also for directing the CO2 product selectivity. The latter is particularly important for Cu catalysts which are known to produce a variety of products with low selectivity. 3a It has, however, been shown by the pioneering work by Hori et al. 3a that, among all catalysts studied, only Cu shows the unique capability to form hydrocarbons, here predominantly C1 (methane) and C2 (ethene, EtOH) products. 4a, 8 Less abundant in the product mixtures of CO2 conversion are hydrocarbons with longer C-chains (e.g. propene 9 ). What makes Cu unique among all CO2 catalysts is its ability to bind the key intermediates of the
electrocatalytic process in a balanced way. The interaction of the catalyst to the *CO ∙ - radical
anion (the asterisk * indicates an adsorption state) as the first reaction intermediate needs to be sufficiently high to allow for the subsequent coupled H + /e - transfer (alternatively direct *H transfer) followed by an OH - abstraction which then leaves adsorbed *CO behind as the second
key intermediate of the CO2 conversion. CO2 catalysts with a low affinity towards *CO ∙ - stabilization (e.g. Sn, Hg, Pb) produce formate as major product by a concerted H + /e - transfer to

the *CO ∙ - radical anion. 10 Also Cu shows a certain tendency towards formate formation, but only
at low overpotentials and moderate CO2 conversion rates. Several authors report FEformate values of even up to 40%. 9, 11
Any improvement of the Cu catalyst, therefore, needs to address the stabilization of the *CO ∙ - by
providing a higher abundance of low-coordinated surface adsorption sites. By this, the
overpotential for the *CO ∙ - might be lowered, the formate pathway might be suppressed which in
turn would then further increase the FEs for the hydrocarbon formation, in particular at low and
moderate overpotentials. We will demonstrate that the Cu catalysts studied herein effectively
suppress the formate pathway in favor of hydrocarbon production.
Once formed, it is the binding energy of the adsorbed *CO which typically decides on the further
reaction pathway. Weakly binding catalysts, such as Au, Ag and Zn easily release CO as major CO2RR reaction product. 3b, 12 Cu, by contrast, binds CO strongly enough which allows for its further reaction into more reduced C1 and C2 products without irreversibly poisoning the catalyst
surface. What now decides on the preference towards the C1 or the C2 pathways is again the abundance of particular surface sites. Both, experimental 13 and theoretical 14 work on single
crystalline Cu catalysts clearly demonstrated that the C-C coupling (C2 pathway) is more
efficient on (100) textured surfaces whereas methane (C1 pathway) is the preferred hydrocarbon
reaction product on (111)-type surfaces. This is why the surface morphology of the Cu catalyst is
considered as an important factor impacting both, activity and product selectivity of CO2 conversion on polycrystalline Cu. 15 Various approaches have been discussed in literature improving the abundance of low-coordinated surface sites on Cu, including sputtering 15 , electropolishing 15 , electrodeposition 16 and anodization 16 . Among them, it is the reduction of surface oxide phases which appear most promising. 17 Frese was the first who reported on a

significantly increased yield of MeOH on thermally formed copper oxide. 18 Li et al. recently
demonstrated that the thickness of the thermally formed Cu2O surface phase is decisive for the resulting CO2RR activity and the durability of the Cu catalyst. 11 This oxide-derived (OD) activation of Cu catalysts is not restricted to CO2 conversion but extends also to the electroreduction of CO. 19
Under in operando conditions during CO2RR at sufficiently cathodic
potentials, it is most likely that the Cu oxide phases undergo a rapid transition into metallic Cu as the actually active CO2 catalyst. 15 It should also be noted that the particular activation of the Cu catalysts by reduction of a precursor is not restricted to the cuprous oxides but extends to other materials such as cuprous halides 3d and cupric carbonates/hydroxides 20 . The oxidation state of the
copper in the precursor material does not seem to play a major role for the catalyst activation as pointed out by Eilert et al.. 20
In this current contribution we combine the above described activation of Cu catalysts via the
reduction of its surface oxide with a novel Cu electrodeposition approach introduced by Shin et al. 21 which produces mesoporous (high surface area) metal foams. The particular porosity could
be carefully controlled by the experimental parameters such as metal ion concentration, pH and deposition time. 21-22 These Cu foams undergo a fast surface oxidation after emersion from the
plating bath. We will demonstrate that these oxide-derived Cu foam catalysts show a superior
selectivity towards C2 product formation at particularly low overpotentials.
2. Experimental Section
Mesoporous Cu foam catalysts were electrodeposited onto planar Cu wafer coupons (Hionix
blanket wafer, provided by BASF SE, Ludwigshafen) that comprise a 100 nm thick PVD Cu seed
layer, a 25 nm thick Ta layer and a 500 nm TOX/SiO2 film on a 5 mm thick Si(100) substrate. The Cu wafer specimens served as substrate for the Cu foam catalyst deposition and as internal
reference for the electrocatalytic CO2RR due its well-defined surface area and highly

reproducible surface morphology (RMS roughness = 1.35 nm, determined by AFM). The PVD
Cu seed is composed by Cu clusters having lateral dimensions in range of 20 – 50 nm (Figure
1a). Cu wafer coupons were used as received. Prior to electrodeposition the wafer coupons
needed to be fixed to a PTFE sample holder with a conductive Cu-tape and subsequently masked
by a chemically resistant silicone-polyester tape. The resulting surface area exposed to the plating bath was Ageo = 1 cm 2 . Thereafter, the sample holder was immersed into a Cu plating bath containing 1.5 M sulfuric acid (ACS grade, H2SO4, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.2 M Cu(II) sulfate solution (ACS grade CuSO4·5H2O, Sigma-Aldrich). The through-mask Cu electrodeposition followed well-established protocols known from literature 9, 21 and were carried out in a glass-
beaker with a Pt-wire serving as counter and a leakless double-junction Ag/AgCl3M as reference electrode. The Pt counter was placed in a glass compartment that was separated from the main cell by a ceramic frit. For the galvanostatic deposition process a current density of J = -3.0 A/cm 2 (normalized to the geometric surface area of Ageo = 1 cm 2 ) was applied for 5, 20, 30, 40, 60 and 80 seconds, respectively, thus resulting into Cu foam catalysts varying in thickness and surface
pore diameter. Figure 1b shows a representative optical micrograph of the black Cu foam catalyst
on the wafer coupon substrate after removal of the square-shaped polymer mask. Before CO2 electrolysis, all Cu foam catalyst catalysts were thoroughly rinsed with Milli-Q water (Millipore,
18.2 MΩ cm, 4 ppb total organic carbon content) and subsequently dried with Ar gas (99.999%,
Carbagas, Switzerland). It should be noted, however, that it is most likely the presence of residual
Milli-Q water which accelerates the surface oxidation of the Cu foam in air (see discussion of the
XRD data below).
In order to determine the FEs of the electroplating process, Cu foam catalysts were chemically
dissolved in 30% HNO3 solution (Sigma-Aldrich) in terms of a through mask dissolution process and subsequently quantified by means of ICP-CRI-MS (Inductively Coupled Plasma

The same ICP-CRI-MS analysis was applied also to the electrolytes after the CO2 electrolysis in order to detect eroded/dissolved Cu catalyst material in solution.
The surface morphology of the Cu foam catalysts was analyzed prior and after CO2 electrolysis by Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM, Hitachi, S-3000N). Surface analysis of the blanket
wafer coupons (reference) was carried out by tapping mode Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM,
Nanosurf Easy Scan II).

Important to note is that the surface area determination is done in a separate measurement
campaign (ideally after the CO2 electrolysis) in order to avoid any cross-contamination originating from the chloride counter-ions of the viologens.
A custom-built, air-tight glass cell (H-type) was used for all voltammetric measurements and CO2 electrolysis experiments. The three-electrode arrangement consisted of a leakless Ag/AgCl3M reference electrode (Metrohm), a bright Pt-foil (15mm x 5mm) serving as counter electrode and
the Cu foam catalysts serving as working electrodes. Possible chloride ion cross-contaminations
in the working electrolytes originating from the Ag/AgCl3M reference electrode were monitored and excluded by ion exchange (IC) chromatography (IC detection limit: 100 ppb Cl). Prior to
electrolysis, the cathodic and the anodic compartments were both filled with 30 ml of 0.5M
NaHCO3 (ACS grade, Sigma-Aldrich) electrolyte solution and saturated with CO2 gas (99.999%, Carbagas, Switzerland). Catholyte and anolyte were separated by a polymer membrane (Nafion
117, Sigma-Aldrich). In order to enhance the CO2 mass transport towards the cathode during electrolysis the catholyte was continuously stirred by magnetic agitation.
All electrochemical measurements (galvanostatic Cu deposition, CV and potentiostatic CO2 electrolysis) were carried out using a potentiostat/galvanostat (Metrohm Autolab 128N, The
Netherlands). The current interrupt approach (Autolab Nova) has been used to determine and
compensate the iR drop. For the sake of comparability, all potentials measured versus Ag/AgCl3M were converted to the RHE scale by using Equation 2:
ERHE (V) = EAg/AgCl(3M) (V) + 0.197 V + (0.059 V × pH) (2)

The pH of the CO2 saturated 0.5 M NaHCO3 solution at the beginning of the electrolysis was determined to be 7.2.
The headspace of the catholyte compartment was continuously purged with CO2 gas thereby transporting volatile reaction products from the headspace into the sampling loops of the gas
chromatograph (GC, SRI Instruments, Multi-Gas Analyzer #3). The partial current density for a given gaseous product was determined using Equation. 3 24 :

where represents the volume fraction of the products measured via online GC using an

involved into the reduction reaction to form a particular product, vm represents the molar CO2 gas flow rate and F the Faraday constant. The partial current density for a given reaction product was

Non-volatile liquid products of the CO2 electrolysis which accumulate in the catholyte during CO2RR were analyzed by means of ion exchange chromatography (Metrohm Advanced Modular Ion Chromatograph: L-7100 pump, Metrosep A Supp 7-250 column, conductivity detector). Further details of the IC analysis can be found in reference 25 .
3. Results and Discussion
Preparation and characterization of the Cu foam catalysts
Cu foam catalysts were electrodeposited on Cu blanket wafer coupons by a through mask plating
process (for technical details see SI, Figure S1) leaving a well-defined area covered with the Cu
foam behind (Figure 1). The basic concept of this template assisted Cu electrodeposition was

adapted from reference 9, 21 and is schematically shown in Figure 2. Since the Cu
electrodeposition takes place under harsh hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) conditions at current densities of J = -3 A cm -2 (1 in Figure 2), hydrogen gas bubbles form at the Cu wafer
substrate and serve as geometric template for the copper plating process which is superimposed
on the HER (2-3 in Figure 2). Cu is deposited in those areas of the substrate only where no
hydrogen bubbles are formed. The process of hydrogen bubble nucleation, growth and
coalescence is a continuous one. As a result of this, a mesoporous Cu film with black appearance
is obtained (Figure 1). The physical origin of the black color is the fine dendritic/fractal structure
of the deposit. Figure 3 shows a representative series of mesoporous Cu foams deposited on the
planar Cu wafer substrate differing in their deposition time. The Cu material surrounding the
pores is not compact but shows instead a less dense and dendritic nature. Such a dendritic growth
mode is expected from experimental conditions where the deposition rate is limited by mass
transport of the metal ions in combination with a reduced mobility of the adatoms on the
emerging electrode surface. Such diffusion limitation is the result of the extremely high (total) current density of J = -3 A cm 2 .
The Faradaic efficiency of the Cu deposition process (FECu) was determined by through-mask chemical dissolution of the Cu foams in 30% HNO3 followed by ICP-CRI-MS analysis (see SI, Figure S1). As shown in Figure 4a there is only a minor increase in the FECu from 30% (5s deposition time) to 37% (100s deposition time). This is why we can describe in a first
approximation the mass of electrodeposited Cu normalized to the geometric surface area as a
linear function of deposition time (Figure 4b).
Along with the total mass of Cu deposited also the film thickness of the Cu foam catalyst
increases linearly with time (Figure 4c). In full agreement with literature we observe an increase of the surface pore diameter with deposition time (Figure 3, Figure 4c). 21 It should be noted,

however, that the pore diameters analyzed at the outermost catalyst surface by top-down SEM
inspection are not representative for the whole Cu foam catalyst. Actually, there is a certain
gradient in pore diameter from the wafer surface towards the outermost surface of the Cu foam.
Furthermore, more funnel-shaped features are formed in particular at longer deposition times due
to the coalescence of individual pores in direction of Cu growth ((4) in Figure 2).
Crucial for any attempt to normalize the electrolysis rate and to calculate area-normalized current
densities are the electrochemically active surface areas of the Cu foam catalysts, denoted in the
following EASA. We attempted to determine the EASA by separate voltammetric measurement
campaigns probing a reversible redox-transition (see SI, Figure S2). For this purpose sweep-rate
depending cyclic voltammograms of the Cu wafer coupon and the foam catalysts were measured
in 10 mM of DMVCl2 (dimethyl-viologen dichloride) solution within the potential range covering the reversible first electron transfer step reducing the di-cationic DMV 2+ to the corresponding mono-cationic DMV •+ radical mono-cation. Based on the fitting of linear Ip vs v 1/2
plots (peak current vs square root of the sweep rate) the electrochemically active surface area was determined as a free fit parameter. The diffusion coefficient of the di-cationic DMV 2+ species required for the fitting was determined by 1 H-DOSY-NMR (see SI, Figure S3). We are aware, however, that the Randles-Sevcik equation 23 was originally derived for an ideal
planar diffusional transport of the redox-active species towards a disc-shaped macroelectrode
surface. This geometric boundary condition is not fulfilled for the Cu foam catalysts. However, our experimental data seem to obey the linear Ip vs v 1/2 relation of the Randles-Sevcik equation (see SI, Figure S2). Furthermore, similar approaches have already been successfully employed to determine the EASA of mesoporous electrode materials. 26 Figure 4d demonstrates a linear
increase of the EASA with deposition time, at least for deposition times below 80s.

The XRD pattern of the Cu wafer and the Cu foam catalysts before CO2 electrolysis (Figure 5a) show (111), (200) and (220) diffraction peaks characteristic for the polycrystalline face centered
cubic (fcc) Cu and its cuprous oxide in agreement with the JCPDS files 46-1043, 00-001-1242
for metallic Cupoly and cuprous Cu2O, respectively. Important to note is that the oxide appears on the Cu foam samples right after electrodeposition indicating that this mesoporous material is
highly sensitive against surface oxidation. Subjecting these catalysts to reductive CO2 electrolysis conditions typically leads to the reduction of the cuprous oxide phases in agreement with Raman spectroscopic data confirming the disappearance of oxide phases under CO2RR conditions. 27 XRD measurements carried out shortly after the CO2RR does not show any significant presence of cupric or cuprous oxides on the catalyst samples (Figure 5b). Similar XRD results have recently been reported by Ren et al.. 27
The XRD characteristics of the reduced Cu foam samples qualitatively resemble those of
polycrystalline bulk Cu. The ideal (calculated) ratios of the peak intensities for polycrystalline Cu
are I200 : I111 = 0.33 and I220 : I111 = 0.05. For the Cu foam we observe a slight deviation from these values with I200 : I111 = 0.35 and I220 : I111 = 0.15. A more pronounce deviation with respect to the ideal polycrystalline case can be observed for the Cu wafer sample where the (200) and the
(220) peaks are only hardly visible or even absent. This observation is pointing out to a more
dominating (111) facet of the Cu clusters, or to their preferential orientation along the (111)
direction.

onto the planar wafer. For that purpose we have chosen the 20s deposition Cu foam (highlighted

green in Figure 3 and Figure 4) with a Cu loading of 25.2 mg cm -2 , a film thickness of 85 µm, a mean surface pore diameter of 52 µm and an EASA of 4.4 cm 2 . Potentiostatic CO2RRs were carried out in the potential range between -0.4 and -1.0 V vs RHE. Corresponding amperometric
current/time traces (see SI, Figure. S4) indicate the reaching of quasi steady-state electrolysis
conditions shortly after an initiation period.
The raising noise level in the current/time traces (see SI, Figure S4) is indicative for an increase
of the gas evolution rate at higher overpotentials. Gas bubbles might be temporarily trapped and
subsequently released into the bulk electrolyte. These temporal variations of the total current density are highest at -1.0 V and are in the order of 5-7 mA/cm 2 (see SI, Figure S4). This trapping
and subsequent release of gas bubbles also ensures a convectional outward transport of
CO2RR/HER products/intermediates through the mesoporous Cu foam into the electrolyte along with a concerted inward transport of reactants (HCO3 - /CO2 and H2O) into the mesoporous catalyst. The readout of steady-state currents was carried out at electrolysis times of 1h and
plotted versus the respective electrolysis potential (Figure 6a). Corresponding quasi-steady-state
linear sweep experiments (LSVs) of the Ar (blanket) and CO2 saturated 0.5M NaHCO3 electrolytes can be found in the Supporting Information (SI, Figure S5).
Filled squares and circles in Figure 6a correspond to the current densities of the planar wafer
surface (red) and the Cu foam catalyst (black), respectively, normalized to the given geometric surface area of Ageo = 1 cm 2 . The observed higher reaction rates on the Cu foam catalysts have to be attributed mainly to the increased electrochemically active surface area as compared to the
planar Cu wafer coupon (Figure 4d). In a first approximation we assume that the EASA of the
wafer is identical to its geometric surface area. If we normalize the steady-state electrolysis
currents with respect to the determined EASA (black circles in Figure 6a), there is only a minor
difference left between the steady-state current densities on the wafer surface and the Cu foam

catalyst. At this point, however, a critical issue of any surface area normalization in context of
CO2 electrolysis needs to be addressed. Both the CO2 electrolysis itself and the parasitic HER are gas evolution reactions where CO/H2 bubbles form at the catalyst surface. Whereas gas bubbles are more readily removed from the planar surface of the planar wafer coupon these bubbles are
temporarily trapped inside the Cu foam catalysts thereby increasing the mean residence time of
these intermediates/products of the CO2RR and the HER inside the catalysts. This effect reduces at the same time the electrochemically active surface area during the CO2 electrolysis and might lead to a significant surface area change inside the Cu foam catalyst that depends on the
morphological characteristics of the catalyst (thickness of the Cu foam; mean surface pore size)
and the applied reaction conditions (e.g. steady-state current density). Although important, these
effects are typically not taken into account for the surface area normalization simply due to a lack
of experimental access to the active surface area under realistic (gas evolution) experimental
conditions. It is important to note that discussions on the specific activity of the (mesoporous)
catalyst with regard to gas evolution reactions (HER, CO2RR) only on basis of voltammetric (see SI, Figure S5) or steady state current data (Figure 6a) are hampered by these circumstances.
An important factor for the evaluation of the catalyst performance besides activity and selectivity
concerns the catalyst stability, in particular when working with mesoporous materials which
might undergo an erosive degradation under massive gas evolution conditions. The Cu foam
catalysts have therefore been analyzed by SEM inspection after 1h electrolysis at -0.4 and -1.0 V
(Figure 6 (b-e)). Irrespective of the applied potential, there are no major changes in the catalyst
morphology visible. In particular the dendritic fine structure of the Cu foam is preserved during
electrolysis. A collapse of the pore structure under massive HER/CO2RR at highest overpotentials of -1.0 V can therefore be excluded. Less severe erosion of Cu material can be
monitored by ICP-CRI-MS analysis of the electrolyte after the 1h electrolysis (see SI, Figure S6).

The observed superior C2 product efficiencies on the Cu foam can be rationalized by a
combination of two particular effects.
The first one is related to the post-deposition treatment of the Cu foam. Room temperature
surface oxidation in the presence of residual water (most likely from the post-deposition cleaning
step) leads to the formation of a Cu2O film which gets electrochemically reduced under CO2RR conditions thereby creating low coordinated surface sites that are particularly active for the C-C
coupling reaction on the Cu. It is interesting to note that such oxide reduction does apparently not
lead in any case to the same active surface site. In case of the thermally oxidized Cu (annealed
Cu) reported by Kanan et al. the product distribution did not get altered significantly compared to the non-annealed polycrystalline Cu. 11

4. Conclusions
We synthesized oxide-derived (OD) Cu foam catalysts for electro-chemical CO2 conversion by an HER assisted electrodeposition process. Our mesoporous catalysts show superior selectivity
towards C2 products formation (C2H4, C2H6). A key step for the conditioning of the Cu foam catalyst is the in operando reduction of the Cu2O phase that has been formed after the Cu electrodeposition. Partial currents assigned to the C2 product formation are intriguingly above the
partial current of the HER at any potential studied (-0.4 V to -1.0V). Highest C2 efficiencies are
observed at -0.8 V, reaching FEC2 = 55%. CO2 electrolysis studies carried on a variety of Cu foam catalysts further demonstrate a strong dependence of the FEC2 values on the surface pore size diameter (thickness of the catalyst). Besides the presence of active surface site favoring the
*CO dimerization, we identify the temporal trapping of gaseous intermediates (CO, H2, C2H4) inside the mesoporous foam as a key factor in particular rationalizing the selectivity towards the
fully reduced C2 product (C2H6). Future in operando spectroscopic studies need, however, to further clarify the underlying atomic-scale mechanism of this enhanced C2 production.
